rounds.text: Univastu India Ltd is fundamentally under-appreciated, backed by a high-conviction rules-based screen score of 93 out of 100 [E65] and exceptional top-line momentum featuring a 132% compounded sales growth over the trailing twelve months [E17] alongside a 245% year-over-year surge [E66]. The company exhibits elite capital efficiency with a Return on Equity of 25.6% [E13] and an ROCE of 30.0% [E12], significantly outperforming the sector median ROCE of 13.6% [E75]. Valuation looks compelling relative to peers, trading at an EV/EBITDA of 11.24x compared to a sector benchmark of 25.32x [E11], and a P/E of 18.41x against its sector benchmark of 27.83x [E6]. Furthermore, a discounted cash flow analysis calculates an intrinsic value of Rs 260 per share, leaving a substantial margin of safety of 48.1% [E45], while a reverse DCF reveals that the current price only implies a modest 9.0% earnings growth compared to the 18.0% base case assumption [E46]. Operational improvements are evident as working capital requirements have successfully dropped from 133 days to 77.6 days [E61], supported by a conservative debt-to-equity ratio of 0.22x [E37] and positive free cash flow of Rs 18 Cr [E35]. Conceded: promoter holding has decreased by 8.63 percentage points down to 64.24% [E40], and debtor days have increased from 71.3 to 128 days [E63].

While the company displays robust headline sales and profit growth, the underlying structural risks and valuation strains demand close scrutiny [E16, E20]. Most critically, promoter holding has dropped significantly from 72.87% in December 2023 to 64.24% by July 2026, representing an insider reduction of 8.63 percentage points [E40]. Operational efficiency is also deteriorating beneath the surface, evidenced by debtor days worsening sharply from 71.3 to 128 days [E63]. Furthermore, operating margins have compressed from 18% three years ago to 14% in March 2026, accompanied by an inconsistent yearly margin trend [E29, E31]. The stock also carries a zero dividend yield despite repeated profitability, alongside elevated annualised volatility of 50.3% and a historical peak-to-trough drawdown of -45.9% [E4, E52, E53, E62]. Conceded: [E14], [E21], [E44].

Conceded: [E40], [E63]. While the bear highlights the drop in promoter stake, insiders still retain a commanding 64.24% majority ownership [E40]. The operational strain of rising debtor days is offset by drastically improved working capital requirements dropping from 133 days to 77.6 days [E61]. Furthermore, the bear's concern over margin compression ignores the more recent positive trajectory, where quarterly operating margin expanded by 3 percentage points year-over-year in March 2026 to 13% [E30], backed by stellar trailing twelve-month sales growth of 132% and profit growth of 282% [E17, E21]. The absence of dividends is a non-issue for growth-focused investors when the company efficiently reinvests its capital to generate a superior ROCE of 30.0% and an ROE of 25.6% [E12, E13, E62]. Finally, historical volatility and drawdowns are eclipsed by a stellar relative-strength rating of 100 and a discounted cash flow intrinsic value pointing directly to a massive 48.1% margin of safety [E45, E50, E53].

Conceded: [E30]. The bull points to a 3 percentage point quarterly operating margin recovery in March 2026, but this arrives alongside an annual operating margin that has eroded from 18% down to 14% over three years, while yearly and quarterly trends are officially categorized as inconsistent [E29, E31, E32]. While the bull dismisses rising debtor days, official metrics show receivables ballooning from 71.3 to a concerning 128 days, directly undermining the claimed working capital efficiency [E61, E63]. The assertion that promoter stake reduction is minor ignores a steady multi-year liquidation where insider ownership dropped by 8.63 percentage points down to 64.24% [E40, E64]. The bull's reliance on a 48.1% margin of safety and a relative-strength rating of 100 overlooks severe technical risks, including an annualized volatility of 50.3% and a historical peak-to-trough drawdown of -45.9% [E45, E50, E52, E53]. Finally, treating a 0.00% dividend yield as standard growth reinvestment contradicts explicit warning flags that the company refuses to pay out despite repeated profits [E4, E62].
